title: MedCoG: Maximizing LLM Inference Density in Medical Reasoning via Meta-Cognitive Regulation
claim: Our method advances the cost-accuracy Pareto frontier and attains far higher inference density than baselines along a fitted scaling curve.
layout: 2 side-by-side scatter plots; left log-cost Pareto, right linear-cost scaling curve
description: Two side-by-side scatter plots share the x-axis of inference cost in dollars per sample. The left panel, titled Inference Cost-Accuracy Analysis, uses a log x-axis. Blue dots mark labeled baselines such as Zero-Shot, CoT, Self-Refine, MultiPersona, AFlow, MedAgents and MedPrompt. An orange solid line shows the Pareto frontier with the method, a dashed blue line shows the frontier without it, and a large red star marks MedCoG-META at the top. A gold dashed arrow near the top, labeled MedCoG-Oracle (upper bound), spans min cost to max cost. The right panel, titled Inference Density Analysis, uses a linear x-axis and a gray dash-dot scaling curve with R²=0.996. A green dashed horizontal arrow from the red star to the curve shows 6.2x inference density, labeled effective cost. A legend sits at lower right. The eye goes first to the red star and the colored annotations.
caption: (a) Inference Cost-Accuracy Analysis based on GPT-4o on 5 hard sets. (b) Inference Density Analysis. The inference scaling curve is fitted with R2 = 0.996. MEDCOG-META advances the Pareto Frontier and shows 6.2× inference density. MEDCOG- ORACLE reveals the upper bound of meta-cognition regulation.
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong potential in complex medical reasoning yet face diminishing gains under inference scaling laws. While existing studies augment LLMs with various knowledge types, it remains unclear how effectively the additional costs translate into accuracy. In this paper, we explore how meta-cognition of LLMs, i.e., their self-assessment of their own cognitive states, can regulate the reasoning process. Specifically, we propose MedCoG, a Medical Meta-Cognition Agent with Knowledge Graph, where the meta-cognitive assessments of task complexity, familiarity, and knowledge density dynamically regulate utilization of procedural, episodic, and factual knowledge. The LLM-centric on-demand reasoning aims to mitigate the diminishing returns under scaling law by (1) reducing costs via avoiding indiscriminate scaling, (2) improving accuracy via filtering out distractive knowledge. To validate this, we empirically characterize the scaling curve and introduce inference density to quantify inference efficiency. Experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and efficiency of MedCoG on five hard sets of medical benchmarks, yielding 6.2x inference density. Furthermore, the Oracle study highlights the significant potential of meta-cognitive regulation.
